options.why: In euthyroid women with antibodies ESHRE specifically recommends not treating (rec. 51).

items.explanation: The ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss guideline considers the evidence on treating subclinical hypothyroidism conflicting: treatment may reduce miscarriage risk, but the potential benefit should be balanced against the risks (rec. 48, conditional).

items.stem: According to the meta-analyses summarised by ATA 2026, how large are the associations of untreated preconception subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH < 10 mU/L) in the general population?

options.text: Conception −14% to −45% and miscarriage +4% to +7%, as absolute differences.
options.why: It multiplies ATA’s figures by ten; they are −1.4% to −4.5% and +0.4% to +0.7%.

options.text: No association with conception, and a 4.5-fold higher miscarriage risk.
options.why: ATA describes slightly lower conception and a small absolute increase in miscarriage, not a 4.5-fold risk.

options.text: Conception −1.4% to −4.5% and miscarriage +0.4% to +0.7%, as absolute differences.
options.why: Correct: small associations, with low-quality studies.

options.text: Conception +1.4% to +4.5% and miscarriage −0.4% to −0.7%, as absolute differences.
options.why: It reverses the direction: conception is slightly lower and miscarriage slightly higher.

items.explanation: According to ATA 2026, untreated subclinical hypothyroidism with TSH < 10 mU/L is associated with a slightly lower chance of conception (−1.4% to −4.5%) and a slightly higher miscarriage risk (+0.4% to +0.7%), with similar figures in assisted reproduction and with low-quality studies. These are small absolute differences.

items.stem: On the relationship between subclinical hypothyroidism and miscarriage, which sentence reflects the difference between ATA 2026 and ASRM 2024?

options.text: Both state that it has no relationship with miscarriage and that screening is unnecessary.
options.why: ATA describes a small increase in miscarriage and asks for TSH in all women with infertility.

options.text: ASRM describes a large increase in miscarriage; ATA asks clinicians to counsel that there is no association.
options.why: It reverses the positions: it is ASRM that asks for counselling that there is no association.

options.text: Both describe the same 50% increase in miscarriage, but only ATA recommends treatment.
options.why: The 50% figure is invented, and ASRM does not describe such an increase.

options.text: ATA describes a slightly higher miscarriage risk; ASRM asks clinicians to counsel that it is not associated with more miscarriage.
options.why: Correct: same literature, opposite conclusions.

items.explanation: ATA summarises a slightly higher miscarriage risk (+0.4% to +0.7% absolute difference) with untreated subclinical hypothyroidism. ASRM recommends counselling that subclinical hypothyroidism and a TSH of 2.5–4.0 mIU/L are not associated with more miscarriage (B, moderate) and considers the evidence insufficient to link it with infertility.

items.stem: For ATA 2026, what is the plausible benefit of treating persistent subclinical hypothyroidism before pregnancy?

options.text: Improving ovarian reserve and increasing the number of oocytes retrieved in IVF.
options.why: ATA does not propose that benefit.

options.text: Preventing progression to overt hypothyroidism, because stimulation and pregnancy increase thyroid demand.
options.why: Correct: this is the plausible benefit ATA points to.

options.text: Making TPOAb negative before transfer and thus reducing the risk of immunological miscarriage.
options.why: ATA does not attribute that effect on antibodies to levothyroxine.

options.text: Doubling the live birth rate, shown in several large high-quality IVF trials.
options.why: ATA cites only one small, low-quality Korean trial of 64 women.

items.explanation: For treatment, ATA cites only one small, low-quality Korean trial (64 women having IVF/ICSI). It considers that the plausible benefit of treating persistent subclinical disease is preventing progression to overt hypothyroidism, especially because ovarian stimulation and pregnancy increase thyroid demand.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman (fictional case) with a TSH of 24 mU/L and low free T4, newly diagnosed, has IVF scheduled next month. According to ATA 2026, what is appropriate?

options.text: Keep the IVF date and start low-dose levothyroxine 25 mcg/day after transfer.
options.why: ATA asks for fertility treatment to be delayed until euthyroidism and uses full dose in overt disease.

options.text: Keep the IVF date without treatment, because levothyroxine is only indicated if TSH exceeds 50 mU/L.
options.why: Invented threshold: ATA states that every woman with overt hypothyroidism planning pregnancy should be treated.

options.text: Start liothyronine, for its faster effect, so as not to delay IVF.
options.why: ATA states that liothyronine should not be used in women planning pregnancy (strong).

options.text: Full-dose levothyroxine (1.5–1.7 mcg/kg/day) and delay IVF until euthyroidism is restored.
options.why: Correct: treatment strong, moderate certainty; delay as a GPS.

items.explanation: ATA 2026 states that every woman with overt hypothyroidism planning pregnancy should be treated with levothyroxine (strong, moderate certainty) and, if newly diagnosed or uncontrolled, that fertility treatment should be delayed until euthyroidism is restored (GPS). Its flowchart uses 1.5–1.7 mcg/kg/day.

items.stem: A hypothyroid patient controlled on desiccated thyroid extract wants to become pregnant. What does ATA 2026 state, and with what grade?

options.text: Keep the extract if TSH is controlled; ATA only suggests switching (conditional, high certainty).
options.why: The recommendation is strong (not conditional) and the certainty low.

options.text: Switch to levothyroxine: desiccated extract and T3 should not be used (strong, low certainty).
options.why: Correct: a strong recommendation with low certainty; strength and certainty are different things.

options.text: Switch to T3 alone, which ATA prefers in women planning pregnancy (strong, moderate certainty).
options.why: ATA states that T3 should not be used in women planning pregnancy.

options.text: Add T3 to the extract to cover the increased demand of pregnancy (GPS).
options.why: ATA states not to use T3 or desiccated extract; demand is covered by increasing levothyroxine.

items.explanation: ATA 2026 states that liothyronine (T3) or desiccated thyroid extract should not be used in women planning pregnancy (strong, low certainty). A recommendation can be strong even when the certainty of evidence is low.

items.stem: According to ETA 2021, which changes explain menstrual disorders in overt hypothyroidism?

options.text: SHBG and total testosterone and estradiol fall, prolactin rises and GnRH may be disturbed; disorders in 25–60%.
options.why: Correct: versus 10% of euthyroid women.

options.text: SHBG and estradiol rise, prolactin falls and GnRH secretion speeds up; disorders in 90%.
options.why: It reverses the changes and the figure is invented: ETA gives 25–60%.

options.text: Only TSH rises, acting directly on the endometrium; disorders in 10%, as in euthyroid women.
options.why: ETA describes changes in SHBG, sex steroids, prolactin and GnRH, with disorders in 25–60%.

options.text: Free testosterone rises through insulin resistance, as in PCOS; disorders in 25–60%.
options.why: The figure is right, but that is not the mechanism ETA describes.

items.explanation: ETA describes that in overt hypothyroidism SHBG and total testosterone and estradiol fall, prolactin rises and pulsatile GnRH secretion may be disturbed, with menstrual disorders in 25–60% versus 10% of euthyroid women. ETA recommends starting levothyroxine promptly in overt dysfunction (R11).

items.stem: A euthyroid woman with infertility has negative TPOAb and a TSH of 3.1 mIU/L. What do ETA 2021 and ATA 2026 say about ordering thyroglobulin antibodies (TgAb)?

options.text: ETA suggests adding TgAb if TSH is > 2.5 with negative TPOAb; ATA leaves them to physician discretion in selected cases.
options.why: Correct: ETA R2 (2, ØØOO) and the ATA text.

options.text: Both strongly recommend ordering TgAb in every woman with infertility, along with TPOAb.
options.why: Neither asks for them in all: ETA suggests them in this situation and ATA leaves them to physician discretion.

options.text: ATA prefers TgAb over TPOAb because they are better associated with reproductive outcomes.
options.why: It is the other way round: for ATA, TPOAb have better accuracy and are associated with worse reproductive outcomes.

options.text: Both advise against TgAb in any circumstance, because they add no information.
options.why: ETA suggests them in this situation, and ATA allows them in selected cases.

items.explanation: ETA 2021 suggests adding TgAb if TSH is > 2.5 mIU/L with negative TPOAb. ATA 2026 considers that TPOAb have better diagnostic accuracy and, unlike TgAb, are associated with worse reproductive outcomes; it leaves TgAb to physician discretion in selected cases, such as a euthyroid TPOAb-negative woman with a high-normal TSH and a high risk of autoimmunity.

items.stem: According to ATA 2026, what is the prevalence of positive TPOAb in women with infertility or after a miscarriage?

options.text: About 40%, four times the general population, and somewhat lower with recurrent miscarriage.
options.why: 40% is the TPOAb proportion among those with subclinical hypothyroidism, not in infertility overall.

options.text: About 1%, much lower than the general population, so they are rarely worth ordering.
options.why: Invented figure: ATA gives 8–11%, similar to the general population.

options.text: About 8–11%, three times the general population, and similar with recurrent miscarriage.
options.why: The figure is right, but ATA describes it as similar to the general population, and perhaps double with recurrent miscarriage.

options.text: About 8–11%, similar to the general population, and perhaps double with recurrent miscarriage.
options.why: Correct: these are the ATA 2026 figures.

items.explanation: ATA 2026 puts the prevalence of positive TPOAb in infertility or after a miscarriage at around 8–11%, similar to the general population, and perhaps twice as high with recurrent miscarriage. It suggests they may be measured in every woman with infertility or recurrent miscarriage (conditional, low certainty).

items.stem: What is ASRM 2024’s position on screening for thyroid autoimmunity?

options.text: It recommends it in every woman with infertility, because TPOAb change the treatment of euthyroid women.
options.why: ASRM does not recommend it in asymptomatic infertile women.

options.text: It recommends it in all pregnant women at the first visit, even without history or symptoms.
options.why: ASRM does not recommend screening in pregnant women either.

options.text: Not in asymptomatic infertile or pregnant women; it may be considered in recurrent loss.
options.why: Correct: C, weak.

options.text: It prohibits it in any circumstance, including recurrent pregnancy loss, for complete lack of evidence.
options.why: ASRM allows it to be considered in recurrent pregnancy loss.

items.explanation: ASRM 2024 does not recommend screening asymptomatic women with infertility or pregnant women for thyroid autoimmunity, although it may be considered in recurrent pregnancy loss (C, weak). ATA suggests they may be measured in every woman with infertility, and ETA recommends them in every subfertile woman.

items.stem: In the trials ATA 2026 relies on (TABLET, T4LIFE and a Chinese IVF trial), in which subgroup of euthyroid TPOAb-positive women did levothyroxine improve outcomes?

options.text: In those with a TSH > 2.5 mU/L before conception.
options.why: No factor modified the response, including a TSH > 2.5.

options.text: In those with previous miscarriages, especially three or more.
options.why: Previous miscarriages did not modify the response either.

options.text: In those with very high TPOAb titres and age over 35.
options.why: Neither TPOAb titre nor age modified the response.

options.text: In none: no factor, including TSH > 2.5, previous miscarriages, age or titre, modified the response.
options.why: Correct: this is how ATA 2026 summarises it.

items.explanation: In the three high-quality trials, preconception levothyroxine did not improve fertility or pregnancy outcomes, and no factor modified the response. ATA takes this to suggest that the higher miscarriage risk is not mediated by thyroid hormone availability, which is why it states levothyroxine should not be offered (strong, high certainty).

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman (fictional case) with three miscarriages, euthyroid and TPOAb positive, asks whether she should take levothyroxine. According to the 2022 ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss guideline, which is correct?

options.text: Yes, with a strong recommendation, because TABLET and T4LIFE showed fewer miscarriages with levothyroxine.
options.why: TABLET and T4LIFE showed no benefit; after them ESHRE recommends not treating.

options.text: Yes, but only if TSH exceeds 2.5 mU/L, according to the recommendation updated in 2022.
options.why: The updated recommendation states not to treat euthyroid women with antibodies, with no TSH exception.

options.text: She should not be treated with levothyroxine (rec. 51, strong, ⊕⊕⊕○), a change made after TABLET and T4LIFE.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE changed its recommendation in 2022.

options.text: It is a free choice: ESHRE makes no statement on levothyroxine in euthyroid antibody-positive women with recurrent miscarriage.
options.why: ESHRE does make a statement, with a strong recommendation not to treat.

items.explanation: ESHRE changed its recommendation in 2022, after TABLET and T4LIFE: euthyroid women with thyroid antibodies and recurrent pregnancy loss should not be treated with levothyroxine (rec. 51, strong, ⊕⊕⊕○). This agrees with ATA 2026.

items.stem: In the trials summarised by ATA 2026, what proportion of euthyroid women with thyroid antibodies developed hypothyroidism within 12 months?

options.text: About 7–9%, mostly before pregnancy but also during it.
options.why: Correct: this is the figure that justifies monitoring every 3–6 months.

options.text: About 50%, almost always in the first month after starting ovarian stimulation.
options.why: Invented figure: ATA gives about 7–9% within 12 months.

options.text: None, because antibodies are not associated with progression to hypothyroidism within a year.
options.why: Some 7–9% developed hypothyroidism within 12 months.

options.text: About 7–9%, but only during pregnancy, never before conception.
options.why: The figure is right, but it occurred mostly before pregnancy.

items.explanation: In the trials, about 7–9% of euthyroid antibody-positive women developed (subclinical or overt) hypothyroidism within 12 months, mostly before pregnancy. That is why ATA suggests rechecking TSH and free T4 every 3–6 months while planning pregnancy (conditional, low certainty).

items.stem: A euthyroid TPOAb-positive woman with recurrent pregnancy loss has just had a positive pregnancy test. What is appropriate according to ESHRE?

options.text: Start preventive levothyroxine 50 mcg/day from the positive test.
options.why: ESHRE does not propose preventive levothyroxine; it proposes measuring TSH and treating if hypothyroid.

options.text: Measure TSH at 7–9 weeks and treat with levothyroxine if she is hypothyroid.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE recommendation 50, a GPP.

options.text: Measure nothing until the second trimester, because TSH cannot be interpreted earlier.
options.why: ESHRE asks for TSH early in pregnancy, at 7–9 weeks.

options.text: Order only monthly serial TPOAb to decide whether to stop monitoring.
options.why: ESHRE does not propose serial antibodies; it proposes TSH at 7–9 weeks.

items.explanation: Once pregnant, ESHRE states that TSH should be checked in early pregnancy (7–9 weeks) in women with thyroid autoimmunity and recurrent pregnancy loss, and hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine (rec. 50, GPP). ATA adds that euthyroid autoimmunity is associated with more miscarriage and with postpartum thyroiditis, which can also follow a miscarriage.

items.stem: Before IVF, a euthyroid TPOAb-positive woman is offered oral prednisolone or intravenous immunoglobulin “for the antibodies”. According to ATA 2026, which is correct?

options.text: They should not be offered to women with thyroid antibodies and infertility (conditional, low certainty).
options.why: Correct: this is what ATA 2026 states.

options.text: They should be offered if TPOAb exceed ten times the limit, with a strong recommendation.
options.why: Invented threshold: ATA states they should not be offered, with no titre exception.

options.text: Only prednisolone is supported, because it reduces miscarriage in high-quality trials.
options.why: ATA states that prednisolone should not be offered, and its text notes there are no supporting data.

options.text: They should be offered if levothyroxine fails, which is the first step with antibodies.
options.why: In euthyroid women with antibodies ATA states that neither levothyroxine nor prednisolone nor immunoglobulin should be offered.

items.explanation: ATA 2026 states that oral prednisolone or intravenous immunoglobulin should not be offered to women with TPOAb and/or TgAb and infertility (conditional, low certainty). Its text summarises that there are no data supporting glucocorticoids, immunoglobulin or selenium to improve obstetric outcomes.

items.stem: What does ETA 2021 say about treatments other than levothyroxine in women with thyroid autoimmunity undergoing assisted reproduction?

options.text: It strongly recommends prednisolone (1, ØØØO) in every TPOAb-positive woman before transfer.
options.why: ETA makes no such recommendation; it frames the topic as a research question.

options.text: It recommends selenium for every antibody-positive woman during ovarian stimulation.
options.why: ETA does not recommend selenium; and ATA advises against selenium in euthyroid antibody-positive pregnant women.

options.text: It expressly advises against them with high-quality evidence, as with levothyroxine.
options.why: ETA does not advise against them: it leaves the question open as a research question.

options.text: It frames it as a research question, not as a recommendation.
options.why: Correct: knowing whether antibodies are an epiphenomenon of a general immune disorder would help decide.

items.explanation: ETA 2021 considers that understanding whether antibodies are an epiphenomenon of a general immune disorder would help determine whether treatments other than levothyroxine could improve assisted reproduction, and frames this as a research question, not a recommendation. ATA 2026 states that prednisolone or immunoglobulin should not be offered.

items.stem: According to ETA 2021, why does TSH rise during ovarian stimulation?

options.text: Because hCG from the trigger directly inhibits pituitary TSH production, which then rebounds.
options.why: This is not the mechanism ETA describes.

options.text: Because gonadotropins stimulate thyroid TSH receptors and exhaust the gland.
options.why: This is not the mechanism ETA describes.

options.text: Estradiol rises to 4,000–6,000 ng/L, TBG increases, free hormone falls and TSH rises.
options.why: Correct: as in the second half of pregnancy.

options.text: Because luteal-support progesterone blocks peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.
options.why: This is not the mechanism ETA describes, which centres on estradiol and TBG.

items.explanation: ETA explains that ovarian stimulation raises estradiol to 4,000–6,000 ng/L, as in the second half of pregnancy: TBG rises, free hormone falls and TSH rises. In about 1 in 3 euthyroid women TSH exceeds 2.5 mIU/L during the cycle, the rise can last 1–3 months and it is greater in treated hypothyroid women.

items.stem: On TSH during ovarian stimulation in euthyroid TPOAb-positive women, which sentence reflects the two guidelines?

options.text: Both describe TSH rising twice as much in TPOAb-positive women.
options.why: ATA describes TSH as comparable with or without TPOAb.

options.text: ETA describes comparable TSH with or without TPOAb; ATA describes higher TSH with TPOAb.
options.why: It reverses the positions of the two guidelines.

options.text: ETA describes higher TSH and lower free T4 with TPOAb; ATA describes comparable TSH with or without TPOAb.
options.why: Correct: this is a disagreement between the sources.

options.text: Neither guideline addresses the influence of TPOAb on TSH during stimulation.
options.why: Both address it, with different conclusions.

items.explanation: The guidelines disagree: ETA describes higher TSH and lower free T4 during stimulation in TPOAb-positive women, whereas ATA 2026 states that in euthyroid women TSH during stimulation is comparable with or without TPOAb.

items.stem: During a cycle with GnRH analogues, a patient (fictional case) reports palpitations, tremor and weight loss. According to ATA 2026, what is appropriate?

options.text: Order no thyroid tests, because ATA always advises against them during stimulation.
options.why: ATA avoids routine tests in that period, but asks for them if thyrotoxic symptoms appear.

options.text: Attribute it to treatment-related anxiety and reassess only if it persists after the pregnancy test.
options.why: ATA warns that analogues can trigger thyroiditis or Graves’ disease, and asks for symptoms to be investigated.

options.text: Start levothyroxine, because stimulation raises TSH and causes these symptoms.
options.why: These are thyrotoxic symptoms, not hypothyroid ones; levothyroxine is not indicated.

options.text: Order thyroid tests: analogues can trigger painless thyroiditis or Graves’ disease.
options.why: Correct: this is the ATA 2026 warning.

items.explanation: ATA considers it sensible not to order thyroid tests during stimulation or within 2 weeks of the trigger, because of physiological changes. But it warns that GnRH analogues or a miscarriage can trigger painless thyroiditis or Graves’ disease, so tests should be ordered if thyrotoxic symptoms appear.

items.stem: A woman with overt hypothyroidism, stable on levothyroxine 100 mcg/day with a TSH of 1.8 mU/L, has a positive pregnancy test after IVF. According to ATA 2026, which is correct?

options.text: Keep the dose until week 20, when most women need the first adjustment.
options.why: Most need an increase of about 25% by week 12; ATA allows raising it on confirming pregnancy.

options.text: It can be raised on confirming pregnancy, by increasing the daily dose or adding two daily doses per week.
options.why: Correct: taking the previous TSH and dose into account to avoid overtreatment.

options.text: Double the dose immediately, because most need a 100% increase by the end of the first trimester.
options.why: Invented figure: ATA describes about 25% by week 12 and 50% by week 20.

options.text: Switch to liothyronine during the first trimester to better meet the needs of fetal neurodevelopment.
options.why: In pregnancy ATA states levothyroxine only, never T3 or desiccated extract.

items.explanation: Most women on levothyroxine for overt hypothyroidism need a dose increase of about 25% by week 12 and 50% by week 20. ATA allows raising it on confirming pregnancy, by increasing the daily dose or adding two daily doses per week, taking the previous TSH and dose into account to avoid overtreatment.

items.stem: A woman taking levothyroxine 25 mcg/day for subclinical hypothyroidism diagnosed before pregnancy has a positive pregnancy test. According to ATA 2026, what is appropriate?

options.text: Apply the standard 25% increase and another of 50% at week 20, as in overt hypothyroidism.
options.why: ATA notes there are no data for applying that standard increase in subclinical disease.

options.text: Stop levothyroxine, because subclinical hypothyroidism no longer needs any treatment in pregnancy.
options.why: ATA does not propose stopping it; it proposes a small or TSH-guided adjustment.

options.text: Switch to full dose of 1.5–1.7 mcg/kg/day, as in newly diagnosed overt hypothyroidism.
options.why: Full dose corresponds to overt hypothyroidism, not to this case.

options.text: A small increase or TSH-guided adjustment, because there are no data for the standard 25% increase.
options.why: Correct: this is what ATA proposes for subclinical disease, based on its writing group’s experience.

items.explanation: The roughly 25% increase is described in women with overt hypothyroidism. In subclinical hypothyroidism diagnosed before pregnancy, ATA notes there are no data for that standard increase and that, based on its writing group’s experience (not a graded recommendation), a small increase or TSH-guided adjustment gives satisfactory results.

items.stem: According to ETA 2021, in which women is TSH measurement recommended after ovarian stimulation?

options.text: In all, including euthyroid women without autoimmunity or levothyroxine, on transfer day.
options.why: ETA does not recommend this check in euthyroid women without autoimmunity not taking levothyroxine (R18).

options.text: Those with autoimmunity on levothyroxine; if pregnant, on the second β-hCG day.
options.why: Correct: ETA R17.

options.text: Only in euthyroid women without autoimmunity, because in treated women TSH is already controlled.
options.why: It reverses the groups: ETA recommends it in women with autoimmunity on treatment, not in euthyroid women without autoimmunity.

options.text: In none, because ETA considers TSH measured after ovarian stimulation uninterpretable.
options.why: ETA does recommend it in women with autoimmunity taking levothyroxine.

items.explanation: ETA 2021 recommends adjusting the dose before stimulation to keep TSH < 2.5 mIU/L (R14) and checking TSH after stimulation in women with autoimmunity taking levothyroxine, on the day of the second β-hCG if pregnant (R17). It does not recommend this check in euthyroid women without autoimmunity unless they are treated with levothyroxine (R18).

items.stem: In a 9-week pregnant woman (fictional case), a TSH of 5.2 mU/L with low free T4 is found for the first time. According to ATA 2026, what is suggested?

options.text: Do not treat and repeat TSH in the third trimester, because TSH is below 10 mU/L.
options.why: The threshold of 10 applies to subclinical disease; with low free T4 it is overt, and ATA proposes confirming within 3 weeks.

options.text: Treat immediately at full dose whatever the TSH, because ATA allows no confirmation of any overt hypothyroidism before treating.
options.why: Treatment without confirmation applies with TSH ≥ 6 mU/L; below that, ATA does allow (conditional) confirming first, within 3 weeks.

options.text: Confirmation within 3 weeks before treating is an option, because TSH is below 6 mU/L.
options.why: Correct: ATA suggests it (conditional, low certainty) when TSH is < 6 mU/L; with TSH ≥ 6 treatment is given without confirmation (strong).

options.text: Give liothyronine, which corrects low free T4 faster in early pregnancy.
options.why: In pregnancy ATA states levothyroxine only, never T3 (strong).

items.explanation: ATA 2026 states that overt hypothyroidism in pregnancy with TSH ≥ 6 mU/L, or persisting on retesting, should be treated (strong, moderate certainty). If new-onset with TSH < 6 mU/L, it suggests confirming it within 3 weeks before treating (conditional, low certainty).

items.stem: In an 8-week pregnant woman (fictional case), mild subclinical hypothyroidism is found. Which sentence reflects the difference between ATA 2026 and ASRM 2024?

options.text: ATA states it should always be treated (strong, high certainty); ASRM too, with a target < 2.5.
options.why: For mild first-trimester disease ATA says it may be treated (conditional), and ASRM does not recommend treatment.

options.text: ATA states it should not be treated (strong, high certainty); ASRM recommends treating it in pregnancy.
options.why: ATA’s strong recommendation not to treat applies to mild disease after the first trimester, and ASRM does not recommend treatment.

options.text: Neither addresses subclinical hypothyroidism in pregnancy.
options.why: Both address it, with different positions.

options.text: ATA says it may be treated (conditional, low certainty); ASRM does not recommend treating it in pregnant women.
options.why: Correct: this is the disagreement between the two guidelines.

items.explanation: According to ATA 2026, mild subclinical hypothyroidism diagnosed in the first trimester may be treated (conditional, low certainty); if diagnosed after the first trimester it should not be treated (strong, high certainty), and with TSH > 10 mU/L it should be treated (GPS). ASRM 2024 does not recommend treating subclinical hypothyroidism with levothyroxine in pregnant women.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman (fictional case) with Graves’ disease receives radioactive iodine and wants to become pregnant. According to ATA 2026, how long should she wait?

options.text: At least 1 month, the time needed to clear the radioactive iodine.
options.why: Invented interval: ATA advises at least six months.

options.text: At least 5 years, because of the malformation risk linked to radiation.
options.why: Invented interval: ATA advises at least six months.

options.text: At least six months, to minimise potential adverse effects of radiation.
options.why: Correct: this is what ATA 2026 advises.

options.text: She need not wait if she switches methimazole to propylthiouracil before treatment.
options.why: Switching antithyroid drug does not remove the interval after radioactive iodine.

items.explanation: If radioactive iodine is given for Graves’ disease before pregnancy, ATA 2026 advises deferring pregnancy for at least six months to minimise potential adverse effects of radiation.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman (fictional case) undergoing infertility work-up has a TSH of 0.2 mU/L with normal free T4. According to ATA 2026, what is appropriate?

options.text: Confirm subclinical hyperthyroidism by rechecking TSH and free T4 after 4–6 weeks.
options.why: Correct: an ATA 2026 GPS.

options.text: Start methimazole immediately, without repeating the test, and keep it throughout pregnancy.
options.why: ATA asks for confirmation first and, when planning pregnancy, proposes propylthiouracil instead of methimazole.

options.why: ATA asks for confirmation first, and after radioactive iodine it advises waiting at least six months.

options.text: Ignore it, because a low TSH with normal free T4 never needs follow-up.
options.why: ATA asks for it to be confirmed by rechecking TSH and free T4.

items.explanation: In women with infertility, ATA 2026 states that subclinical hyperthyroidism should be confirmed by rechecking TSH and free T4 after 4–6 weeks, and overt hyperthyroidism treated before conception according to its cause or with low-dose antithyroid drugs if none is found (both GPS).

items.stem: A 37-year-old woman (fictional case) with Graves’ disease controlled on antithyroid drugs is going to freeze oocytes, with no transfer planned soon. Which is correct according to the sources?

options.text: She must stop the antithyroid drug during stimulation, because it interferes with oocyte maturation.
options.why: ATA states the antithyroid drug can be continued during preservation.

options.text: She must receive radioactive iodine before stimulation so as not to need antithyroid drugs.
options.why: No source proposes this, and after radioactive iodine ATA advises waiting at least six months for pregnancy.

options.text: She can continue the antithyroid drug during preservation; ETA asks for risks to be explained before assisted reproduction.
options.why: Correct: ATA 2026 (text) and ETA 2021 (abstract).

options.text: She must switch to liothyronine during stimulation to avoid hypothyroidism from high estradiol.
options.why: It makes no sense in hyperthyroidism, and ATA states T3 should not be used in women planning pregnancy.

items.explanation: If only oocyte or embryo cryopreservation is planned with no transfer soon, ATA allows antithyroid drugs to be continued during preservation. ETA 2021 asks for a subfertile woman with hyperthyroidism planning assisted reproduction to be informed of the higher risk of maternal and fetal complications, and for euthyroidism to be restored and maintained for several months before treatment.

items.stem: According to ATA 2026, what daily iodine intake should pregnant and breastfeeding women aim for, and what ceiling does it set for pregnancy?

options.text: 150 mcg/day in total, avoiding more than 250 mcg/day.
options.why: 150 mcg/day is the suggested supplement dose, not total intake; the ceiling is 500 mcg/day.

options.text: 250 mcg/day from supplements only, not counting diet, with no ceiling set.
options.why: ATA counts diet plus supplements and sets a ceiling of 500 mcg/day.

options.text: 500 mcg/day from diet and supplements, avoiding more than 1,000 mcg/day.
options.why: 500 is the ceiling, not the target; the target is 250 mcg/day.

options.text: 250 mcg/day from diet and supplements, avoiding sustained intake above 500 mcg/day.
options.why: Correct: both strong, with moderate certainty.

items.explanation: ATA 2026 recommends that pregnant and breastfeeding women aim for a daily iodine intake of 250 mcg, from diet plus supplements as needed (strong, moderate certainty), and avoid sustained intake or supplements above 500 mcg/day in pregnancy (strong, moderate certainty).

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman (fictional case) in Spain, on levothyroxine and without dietary restrictions, is planning pregnancy and asks about iodine. Which is correct according to ATA 2026?

options.text: The table suggests 150 mcg/day for women at risk of deficiency; the text extends it to all, unless intake is high.
options.why: Correct: and the same recommendations apply with levothyroxine.

options.text: Levothyroxine exempts her from iodine, because it already supplies the iodine the fetal thyroid needs.
options.why: ATA suggests applying the same iodine recommendations to pregnant women taking levothyroxine.

options.text: ATA gives data showing Spain has no iodine deficiency, so she needs no supplement.
options.why: The guideline gives no data on iodine status in Spain or Argentina.

options.text: The ATA table strongly recommends 150 mcg/day for all women, without exception.
options.why: The table restricts the suggestion (conditional) to women at risk of deficiency; it is the text that extends it.

items.explanation: The ATA 2026 table suggests a 150 mcg/day supplement for women at risk of deficiency from region, dietary restrictions or malabsorption, ideally from at least 3 months before pregnancy (conditional, moderate certainty); the text extends it to all, unless dietary intake is high. It suggests applying the same to those on levothyroxine (conditional, low certainty). The guideline gives no data on Spain or Argentina.

asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism.title: Subclinical hypothyroidism in the infertile female population: a guideline
asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine
asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism.population: Women with infertility or miscarriage and pregnant women, in relation to subclinical hypothyroidism. Replaces the 2015 ASRM version.
asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism.finding: Use the laboratory TSH cut-offs; if unavailable, 4.12 mIU/L for non-pregnant women and those attempting pregnancy (B; moderate). Counsel that subclinical hypothyroidism and a TSH of 2.5–4.0 mIU/L are not associated with more miscarriage (B; moderate). Treating subclinical hypothyroidism with levothyroxine in women desiring pregnancy or pregnant is not recommended (B; moderate). Test TSH and T4 when there are signs or symptoms of hypothyroidism (including irregular cycles), not in all infertility patients (B; moderate). Do not screen asymptomatic women for thyroid autoimmunity; it may be considered in recurrent pregnancy loss (C; weak).
asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism.limitations: Full PDF read (Fertil Steril 2024;121:765-82). Strength of evidence A/B/C and strength of recommendation strong/moderate/weak. Much of its position rests on an influential trial having data-integrity concerns. US context.

ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.title: American Thyroid Association 2026 Guidelines for Thyroid Disease in Preconception, Pregnancy, and Postpartum
ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.authors: Korevaar TIM, Leung AM, Alexander EK, Bliddal S, Boelaert K, Brenta G, Chou R, Dhillon-Smith R, Dosiou C, Eaton JL, Guan H, Kilpatrick SJ, Lasserre BJ, Lee SY, Maraka S, Meister KD, Morris-Wiseman LF, Nguyen CT, Pearce EN, Shan Z
ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.population: Women planning pregnancy (including those with infertility, recurrent miscarriage or fertility treatment), pregnant women and women postpartum or breastfeeding. Replaces the 2017 ATA guideline; endorsed by, among others, ESHRE, the European Thyroid Association, ACOG, the Endocrine Society and the Latin American Thyroid Society.
ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.finding: Infertility: TSH for all women with infertility or recurrent miscarriage (GPS) and optional TPOAb (conditional, low); on levothyroxine, target TSH 0.5–2.5 mU/L (GPS). Subclinical hypothyroidism: confirm after 4–6 weeks (conditional, moderate); TSH > 10 mU/L, treat (GPS); if persistent, low-dose levothyroxine (25–75 mcg/day; 25–50 in flowchart 1) (conditional, low certainty). Euthyroid autoimmunity (TPOAb and/or TgAb): do not offer levothyroxine (strong, high), recheck TSH and FT4 every 3–6 months; no prednisolone or immunoglobulin. Pregnancy: without a laboratory-specific interval, TSH 0.1–4.0 mU/L in the first and second trimesters. Iodine: 250 mcg/day total intake in pregnancy and lactation (strong, moderate); 150 mcg/day supplement in women at risk of deficiency (conditional, moderate); avoid > 500 mcg/day. Do not offer selenium to euthyroid antibody-positive pregnant women (conditional, moderate).
ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.limitations: Full text read in the published version deposited in the University of California repository (eScholarship). Recommendations carry no individual number: they are cited by their “Recommendations Table” and page. Strength strong (“should”) or conditional (“may”), GRADE certainty very low to high, or good practice statement (GPS). The authors acknowledge that much of the evidence is of low or moderate quality; dissenting comments from group members are in supplementary material that was not reviewed. It gives no data specific to Argentina or Spain.

eshre-2022-rpl.title: ESHRE guideline: recurrent pregnancy loss: an update in 2022
eshre-2022-rpl.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on RPL; Bender Atik R, Christiansen OB, Elson J, et al.
eshre-2022-rpl.population: Couples with recurrent pregnancy loss (two or more losses).
eshre-2022-rpl.finding: Low-dose folic acid has not been shown to prevent loss in unexplained RPL (strong); do not use high doses without hyperhomocysteinaemia or conditions raising NTD risk (diabetes, epilepsy). Prophylactic vitamin D may be considered in preconception counselling (GPP) although evidence of effectiveness is absent; vitamin D testing to find a cause is not recommended. Multivitamins: advise options safe in pregnancy (GPP); they are not a treatment. Sperm DNA fragmentation in couples with RPL: could be considered for diagnostic purposes, using a validated test (conditional; ⊕⊕⊕○). Parental karyotyping: not routine; can be carried out after an individual risk assessment (conditional).
eshre-2022-rpl.limitations: Recommendations table and vitamin D chapter read in the full ESHRE PDF. Specific RPL population; several recommendations are good practice points (GPP), not trial-based. Recommendations on sperm DNA fragmentation and parental karyotyping checked in the HRO summary (hoad002) and in the justification of the full PDF.

eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.title: Evidence-based guideline: unexplained infertility
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Unexplained Infertility; Romualdi D, et al.
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.finding: With regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to identify the aetiology of infertility or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong recommendation, low certainty). IUI with ovarian stimulation first line (strong, very low certainty). ICSI not recommended over conventional IVF (rec. 42, strong, ⊕); endometrial scratching should not be offered (rec. 45, strong, ⊕⊕); adjunct oral antioxidants in women probably not recommended (rec. 46, conditional, ⊕).
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.limitations: Search up to October 2022; many recommendations with low or very low certainty. Full text read (journal summary via Europe PMC PMC10546081 and the full 114-page ESHRE guideline).

eta-2021-thyroid-art.title: 2021 European Thyroid Association Guideline on Thyroid Disorders prior to and during Assisted Reproduction
eta-2021-thyroid-art.authors: Poppe K, Bisschop P, Fugazzola L, Minziori G, Unuane D, Weghofer A
eta-2021-thyroid-art.population: Women and men in subfertile couples, before and during assisted reproduction (IVF/ICSI), in the European context. Aimed at endocrinologists and gynaecologists.
eta-2021-thyroid-art.finding: Screen TSH and TPOAb in every woman seeking advice for subfertility (R1; 1, ØØØO); TgAb if TSH > 2.5 mIU/L with negative TPOAb (R2). Defines subclinical hypothyroidism as TSH > 4.0 mIU/L or above the assay upper limit if that is higher; treat with levothyroxine to keep TSH < 2.5 mIU/L, with or without autoimmunity (R12, R13; 1, ØØOO). With autoimmunity and TSH between 2.5 and 4.0, low-dose levothyroxine (25–50 µg) case by case (R15; 2, ØØOO). Do not systematically treat euthyroid women with autoimmunity undergoing IVF/ICSI (R19; 2, ØØOO). Check TSH after stimulation in women with autoimmunity on levothyroxine (R17).
eta-2021-thyroid-art.limitations: Full text read on the PubMed Central HTML page (no pagination). Grades: 1 = strong recommendation, 2 = weak or suggestion; ØOOO very low to ØØØØ high quality. It predates ATA 2026 and the T4LIFE trial (2022), although it already includes TABLET and the Chinese IVF trial; its thresholds and its case-by-case levothyroxine stance in euthyroid autoimmunity differ from later guidelines.

nice-2026-ng257.title: Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (NG257)
nice-2026-ng257.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng257.population: People with fertility problems in the UK health system.
nice-2026-ng257.finding: Do not use AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3). Use AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4). Do not use FSH as a predictor (1.18.5). Refer at presentation if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factors (1.16.8); otherwise investigation after 1 year of unprotected intercourse. Unexplained fertility problems: keep trying for 2 years in total before treatment (1.38.1); do not offer ovarian stimulation as a stand-alone treatment (1.38.2); then consider up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophins or offer IVF (1.38.3). Male factor: repeat an abnormal semen analysis, ideally at 3 months (1.17.4); do not test sperm DNA fragmentation (1.17.6); do not offer androgens (1.24.3). Endometriosis: expectant management for up to 2 years (including time already spent trying) or surgery; then consider up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophins or offer IVF (1.36.1–1.36.3). Add-ons: do not offer endometrial scratch or hysteroscopy as pre-treatment (1.40.1–1.40.2), endometrial receptivity testing (1.41.1), immunological agents (1.42.1) or PGT-A (1.48.1); do not offer assisted hatching (1.49.1, from 2004); ICSI: offer with surgically retrieved sperm or frozen–thawed oocytes, consider with abnormal semen or previous failed fertilisation, and do not use without male factor (1.50.1–1.50.5).
nice-2026-ng257.limitations: NHS (UK) context; replaces CG156. Numbering checked in the March 2026 PDF.
